items.title: Four evaluation engineering lessons learned from building agent plugins
items.author: Casey West Developer Relations Lead, AI Infrastructure & Applied Engineering, Google Cloud
items.summary: The real challenge of building an agentic system isn't the construction, it's the measurement. Evaluation engineering is a critical foundation for building reliable AI systems. Setting up systematic, repeatable tests to measure your agent’s true behavior can be the difference between shipping a tool you can trust and one that silently breaks, fails to call APIs, or makes mistakes. I’ve run evaluation engineering initiatives for years at Google and d eveloping the newly released Google Cloud Developer plugin served as a live testbed to stress-test these key principles across real-world developer workflows. Here are four eval lessons we learned from building the new plugin that you can apply to your own builds. 1. Grade the execution steps instead of the summary When we first evaluated agents, we set up an LLM-as-judge to inspect the agent’s final text reply and scored it against a checklist. However, we quickly realized it’s fundamentally flawed because the grader only sees what the agent wrote, not what it actually did. When we ran our initial 11-prompt evaluation suite for the Google Cloud Developer plugin, the automated grader marked it as failing three prompts. But when we opened the raw tool-call logs and read the transcripts, the plugin had actually passed all three. On a Cloud Run cleanup prompt, for instance, our rubric required checking command syntax before running anything. The agent ran gcloud help run services list as its very first step. It did the work, but its final message was focused on warning the user about permanent data loss rather than reciting that it had checked the help docs. The grader penalized the agent for doing the right thing simply because it didn’t brag about it in the summary. If your rubric line says "did it run X?", a LLM judge is guessing unless you evaluate the actual tool-call trajectory. Takeaway : Don't grade an agent on its closing pitch. Score the raw execution trajectory to verify what commands were actually executed, validated, and scoped. 2. Design evals for asynchronous operations When you start reading tool-call trajectories, how you extract that telemetry matters just as much as what you're reading. Extracting agent telemetry into a flattened, sequential list of events obscures concurrent tool dispatch, which is one of the critical causes of behavioral failure. Modern agent harnesses often batch multiple tool invocations into a single assistant turn using an array of calls. In our evaluations, when an agent was asked to inspect an environment and look up documentation, the harness dispatched the skill-loading call and two documentation searches simultaneously within a single tool_calls payload. Because activating a skill is a multi-stage process, where the initial call returns a short launch stub and the subsequent turn injects the full instruction body, the instructions meant to govern the search arrived in the prompt context after the system had already executed the searches. The system never gave the skill a dedicated turn to let its guidance influence the agent's actions. If telemetry pipelines strip out turn structures and merge calls into a flat timeline, engineers will waste days wondering why an agent disregarded unambiguous instructions that a developer embedded in a skill. Takeaway : Preserve turn structure in telemetry extractors so you can identify when client-side parallel dispatch issues tool calls before injected guidance enters the context window. 3. Test live runs and "dry runs" side-by-side You need to inspect real API calls to catch harness quirks, like parallel dispatch. But if you only test your agent in one environment condition, you're flying half-blind. From day one, you need to run two conditions side-by-side: a live run and a plan-only run. In the live condition, the agent has real, sandboxed credentials and actually executes commands. This is how you see if syntax works, parameters serialize cleanly, and the agent exercises restraint before doing something destructive. Live runs frequently hit an unexpected permission error on step two and abort before you ever reach the behavior you’re trying to test. That's why you need the plan-only condition, where you strip credentials and tell the agent to explain what it would do without running anything. This strips out permission roadblocks and shows you the model’s pure reasoning and routing intent. Roughly half our most important findings came from the delta between the two. For example, on one of our onboarding prompts, a live run was blocked immediately on a project list call. The plan-only run sailed right through and produced an 8,000-character plan that completely ignored organization policies, admin approvals, and governance. The live run masked a major cognitive flaw that the plan-only run exposed in seconds. Takeaway : Run live and plan-only evaluations side by side. Live runs test actual execution and safety restraint; plan-only runs expose the model's raw reasoning and routing without getting tripped up by permission errors. 4. Use “golden sets” as durable baselines Frontier model architectures change every few months, agent harnesses improve, and plugin manifest standards will inevitably evolve. When building the Google Cloud Developer plugin, we treated evaluations as continuous integration testing for these non-deterministic environments. That means we stress-tested the composite stack, including the harness, the live model, and the tools running together on realistic tasks. Instead of guessing from the final text output, this approach captures the whole trajectory: what the agent thought, what commands it actually ran, and whether it solved the problem without breaking anything. Then you score that run against golden sets curated by real human experts who know what the ideal path looks like. Takeaway : Build golden sets based on what the entire system should actually do in the wild, including your harness, model, and plugins. Models change, but those baseline runs are your safety net. Reminder: Use evaluation suites over “one-shot” demos A common mistake I see among engineers is what I like to call the one-shot demo. This is when someone feeds a prompt into a LLM, watches it build a complete 3D game or solves a Rubik’s cube in a single pass and calls it an eval. But in reality, this is just a vanity metric. To do quality work with AI, I truly believe that you need evaluation suites. Without evaluations, teams are like literally running into a dark cave blind. Engineering an enterprise-grade agent means testing the system's ability to handle multi-step interactions, manage permissions, and avoid destructive outcomes like accidentally deleting a project because you asked it to "find opportunities to save costs." Where to go from here Building an agent plugin or MCP server is the beginning. Shipping something you can actually trust with real cloud infrastructure requires significantly more work in evaluations to ensure it’s doing what you expect it to do. At the end of the day, the only thing that outlasts model churn is a stress-tested eval suite. Check out the Google Cloud Developer plugin documentation or explore this codelab to get started with the plugin in Antigravity.

items.title: Architecting autonomy: A design pattern for high-compute, governed agents in biotech
items.author: Schneider Larbi Sr. Manager, Global Partner Technical Architecture
items.summary: In production systems today, most AI agents operate as lightweight dispatchers. They parse a prompt, make an API call, retrieve a record, and hand back control. Their execution is fast, stateless and cheap. Biotechnology does not work this way. Folding a protein target, screening a 50,000 compound ligand library, or evaluating structure-activity relationships (SAR) are not quick API lookups. They are sustained, stateful, GPU-bound simulations that run for minutes or even hours across specialized silicon. When you ask a general-purpose large language model (LLM) endpoint to coordinate a complex drug discovery workflow, the standard paradigm breaks: Timeouts occur, context windows overflow with atomic coordinates, and proprietary chemical Intellectual Property (IP) risks exposure to external networks. Building enterprise grade research and development (R&D) agents requires moving past the monolithic assistant model. In this blog post, we will discuss how to use a three-layer architecture: separating cognitive orchestration (the brain) from computational execution (the muscle), and anchoring both inside an enterprise governance plane to build scalable agents for drug discovery use cases in biotech. A three-layer pattern The reference architecture below shows how to architect, optimize, and govern high-compute autonomous agents in biotechnology, specifically Drug Discovery. Figure 1 — The three-layer pattern: a cognitive orchestrator (brain), a scalable GPU execution layer (muscle), and an enterprise governance plane. The execution layer: scaling the muscle - high-compute execution The execution layer is responsible for the heavy scientific computations. The first architectural decision is determining where workloads should run: Strategic, proprietary pipelines require dedicated GPU infrastructure within your security perimeter Routine or standardized workloads can safely be delegated to managed cloud endpoints In this architecture, protein folding is driven by ESMFold and generative design by GenMol . Both run as NVIDIA Inference Microservices or NIMs deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) using G4 VMs backed by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. A critical hurdle in containerized GPU workloads is the cold-start penalty, the latency delay required to pull multi-gigabyte model weights from an image registry and stage them into GPU memory (VRAM). To ensure low latency responsiveness, we build the following as a recommendation into the reference architecture: Maintain warm pools: Pin the GKE node pool to a minimum of one active node. Preload weights: Model weights are loaded directly into VRAM at pod initialization, ensuring containers are immediately ready for inference. Resilient scheduling: GKE manages pod lifecycles and restarts failed instances without tearing down the underlying VM infrastructure. This approach trades custom, manual CUDA kernel tuning for NVIDIA's pre-compiled, containerized runtimes, dramatically reducing infrastructure engineering overhead while ensuring deterministic throughput. In biotech, chemical structures represent millions of dollars in proprietary IP. A docking request transmits SMILE strings or 3D coordinate matrices that must never leave company custody. Containerized NIMs eliminate the friction between rapid prototyping and rigorous data isolation. During early exploration, researchers can query NVIDIA hosted endpoints. When transitioning to proprietary lead candidates, the exact same container is deployed to GKE inside a private VPC . The agent’s orchestration logic remains identical; only the target URI updates from an external proxy to an internal VPC endpoint. No structural data leaves the enterprise perimeter. The cognitive layer: Multi-agent reasoning With compute execution isolated, the cognitive layer manages agentic workflow sequencing. Built on Agent Runtime , within the Gemini platform, this reference architecture shows a system that deploys a hierarchical multi-agent structure, one lead orchestrator, and two specialized domain sub-agents (Lead Optimization and Safety Screening) . The multi-agent design can be modified to suit the use case at hand. Based on this design, when an end-user submits a high-level task such as “ Analyze Candidate 4b against Target X and produce a SAR report” , the system applies four core orchestration patterns discussed below; In-process native agent handoffs: The lead orchestrator delegates tasks to specialist sub-agents using Agent Runtime’s native SDK rather than network-serialized agent-to-agent HTTP protocols. This eliminates intermediate network hops and keeps internal handoffs instantaneous. Only the outermost boundary communicates outward to user-facing surfaces like the Gemini agent. Passing bulky payloads by reference: LLMs degrade quickly when forced to ingest massive arrays of 3D spatial coordinates. In this architecture, raw structural data (PDB files, docking poses, trajectory logs) is written directly to Cloud Storage . Agents pass lightweight, signed object URIs and high-level structural summaries, keeping context windows compact and inference costs down. Decoupling workflow logic from biochemical reasoning: General-purpose LLMs excel at task planning and synthesis, but are prone to hallucinating biochemical nuances. To control this behavior, this architecture maintains strong separation of concerns, namely, workflow and tasks decomposition are handled by Gemini. Domain chemistry and pharmacological reasoning are handled by specialized Nemotron models hosted on dedicated GPU nodes. Context-driven evaluation over rigid cutoffs: Traditional computational screening enforces arbitrary numerical cutoffs (e.g., discard if binding affinity ,-7.5 kcal/mol) However, therapeutic context fundamentally alters risk tolerance. Preventive cardiovascular therapy taken daily by healthy patients requires extremely strict safety margins, or a novel oncology candidate targeting an intractable cancer may accept higher toxicity if efficacy is demonstrated. By passing disease context directly into the specialized reasoning models, drug candidates are evaluated against dynamic, target-specific profiles rather than static thresholds, preventing the premature culling of viable drug leads. Performance best practices for high-compute pipelines Optimizing an agentic system that interfaces with heavy GPU compute requires challenging common engineering instincts: Common Assumption Architectural Reality Recommended Best Practice "Swap in a faster driver model to cut latency." The primary orchestrator's token generation is rarely the bottleneck in multi-step R&D pipelines. Optimize I/O, not token speed: Focus on reducing payload sizes and intermediate network hops rather than compromising orchestrator reasoning depth. "Parallelize tool calls across workers." External scientific services and containerized models often serialize requests internally on dedicated hardware. Respect execution topology: Align client-side concurrency with backend queue mechanics to prevent pipeline lockouts and connection timeouts. "Pass full simulation states between tools." Large JSON bodies cause schema validation failures, prompt truncation, and token bloat. Pass heavy payloads by reference: Store raw coordinates in object storage and pass lightweight URIs between agent boundaries. "Return outputs only when the pipeline finishes." Long multi-minute runs leave scientists blind to whether jobs are proceeding or stalled. Stream intermediate stage completions: Emit progress updates at each completed milestone (e.g., folding complete , docking running ) for real-time visibility. "Chain multiple granular micro-tools." Deep tool-chains increase the probability of hallucinated arguments and schema mismatches. Collapse compute pipelines: Wrap end-to-end simulation pipelines behind a single, clean tool interface that takes clear parameters and returns a consolidated object. The enterprise governance and asymmetric autonomy Deploying high-compute agents in enterprise environments requires robust data sovereignty, audit trails, and process control. The Gemini platform establishes these safeguards natively with the following components: Agent Identity : Every autonomous agent operates with a cryptographically verifiable identity. Thus, for a biotech use case, when a candidate molecule is advanced or rejected, the event is permanently logged to that specific agent principal. Agent Gateway : This serves the single ingress/egress point for every interaction within the perimeter. Centralized IAM and regional residency rules help ensure sensitive molecular data remains within designated cloud regions. Agent Registry : This feature maintains a curated catalog of approved agents, validated tool schemas, and authorized Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, preventing rogue tools from executing in production. Model Armor : This functionality inspects incoming prompts and outgoing payloads in real time to prevent prompt injection and data exfiltration. The payoff is clear. Identity, RBAC, auditing, residency, and data protection are native properties of the Gemini platform; this allows enterprise customers to focus on science rather than having to build a compliance stack for every project. In high-stakes research and development, full autonomy introduces unacceptable liability, while requiring approval for trivial steps can create frictions. The solution addressing this to use asymmetric gating in the following ways; Automate reversible operations: For example, allow the agent to resolve chemical naming synonyms, pull structural PDBs, and run preliminary Lipinski screens autonomously without interrupting the researcher. Gate irreversible operations: For instance, initiating multi-GPU docking run, advancing a lead compound to wet-lab synthesis, or archiving a therapeutic program must require explicit human sign-off. The pattern, and the path forward High-compute autonomous agents succeed when the boundaries between cognitive planning, numerical computation, and system governance are clean in the following ways: Keep the orchestrator focused on decomposition and synthesis, leaving intensive biophysical simulation to specialized, containerized microservices and models. Eliminate context bloat by passing complex chemical data by reference through cloud storage. Anchor the workflow in enterprise governance, pairing cryptographic agent identity with asymmetric human oversight. As generative and structural biology models expand toward whole-cell modeling and complex dynamic simulations, this decoupled architecture ensures research systems scale efficiently while keeping proprietary IP secure and auditable. Reach out to your Google sales representative if you have any requirements to build a use case like this and we will be happy to talk and support you in your agent development journey on Google Cloud.

items.title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
items.author: Andy Riancho
items.summary: In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox , inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture. Here is a summary of the challenge: 1,285 reports over two weeks $242,000 in bounties paid out One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel. The kernel zero day The program's most important report arrived on day three. Paulos Yibelo (pwn.ai), a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks: Leak host memory over the network Crash the host machine Execute code on the host Leaking host memory In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending. This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes. Crashing the host and executing code on the host The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host. First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary. The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration. Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk. Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe. The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public. Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation. Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture. Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes. The white-box deep dive Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code. They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant. On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented: Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach. One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes. Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host. Vercel Sandbox findings We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed. Here is a breakdown of reports by category: 877 duplicates 319 not applicable 57 valid 32 informative In our report triage we have validated: 1 Critical finding 5 High findings 9 Medium findings 42 Low findings 32 Informative findings We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties. The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should. The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data. We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu. That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced. Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits) Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement. When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum} . The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative. The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem. The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings. The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary. Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles. The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs. Thank you to the research community We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox. Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance. Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation . Read more

items.title: Unblock agentic software delivery with governed code review
items.author: Stuart Moncada https://about.gitlab.com/blog/authors/stuart-moncada/
items.summary: AI agents have changed how much code a team can produce in a day. Review queues haven’t kept up, and delivery stalls while changes wait for a closer look. The usual workarounds (reminders, reviewer rotations, assigning a team) buy a little time and then burn people out. Client-side review with AI helps the author by catching issues as the code is being written, before a merge request even opens. But it only goes so far. A review that only checks quality still leaves the organization without enforceable policy on the way to production, since comments on a diff do not decide whether a change can merge or reach production. Every merge request still needs a consistent certification step tied to pipelines, security findings, code owners, approval rules, and audits. Review in the author’s environment cannot standardize that work across all your projects, route policy-bound changes to the right person, or show leaders what the agent did before the change merges. As agents write more of the code, automated reviews need to happen in the platform that already tracks each change from plan to production, and where identity, policy, and oversight controls are already in place. Earlier this year, we made Code Review Flow generally available on GitLab Duo Agent Platform , bringing that sign-off to the merge request and making agentic review part of the same platform where code ships. Teams can turn it on so every change is automatically addressed under rules you set once, at $0.25 per review, delivering an estimated 100x ROI . That predictable unit cost is low enough to leave automatic review on for every merge request, which is how reviews move at machine speed while staying cost-efficient at organizational scale. Agentic reviews, built for how you ship Code Review Flow is native to GitLab merge requests, so it covers your whole environment. It runs as a CI/CD job on your runners, whether GitLab-hosted or your own, so review executes in the same environment as the rest of delivery. It works the same way on GitLab.com, GitLab Dedicated, and GitLab Self-Managed, keeping inference under your control with self-hosted models when air-gapped or regulated environments require it. You also have the flexibility to choose which model acts as the foundation for agentic code review: GitLab-managed or your own self-hosted models. When certification is the default on the merge request, teams get coverage, control, and follow-through in one place. Here are the key highlights for agentic code review with GitLab Duo Agent Platform: Every merge request is reviewed, without anyone having to ask. Turn on automatic reviews at the project, group, or instance level and settings cascade. Authors don’t have to remember to request a first pass. Standards you set once for how the group ships. Custom review instructions capture language conventions, security practices, and path-specific rules. A group can point the Code Review Flow at a template project so those standards travel with the work. Pair guidance with GitLab’s enforced security and compliance controls when a requirement must always hold. Follow-through on every finding. Follow-up review rechecks what GitLab Duo Agent Platform already flagged, verifies fixes, and avoids repeating the same points. At that price, you can leave automatic reviews everywhere. The right human, when policy requires one. Code owners and relevant approval rules still apply. Recommend Reviewers Flow suggests the smallest group that can satisfy those rules based on their level of expertise, workload, availability, and timezone. How agentic code review works in GitLab Within GitLab, code review happens on the merge request, next to your pipelines, security findings, and approvals. A merge request opens (or becomes ready). Automatic review can start the Code Review Flow, or an author assigns GitLab Duo. The flow runs as a CI/CD job on your runners, analyzes the change with repository and merge request context, guided by your custom review instructions and the models your group selected, and comments on the diff. Authors and their coding agents push fixes. Follow-up review verifies Duo’s prior findings and carries context forward from the earlier pass. When a human must approve, Recommend Reviewers Flow proposes who should take the request; you assign from the merge request. Pipelines, security findings, approval rules, and the session record stay in the same place, so “reviewed” means certified on the path to production. Watch agentic code review in GitLab in action: What’s ahead Our platform roadmap for agentic code review includes: Deeper review when the change warrants it. An extended analysis pass will pull in calling code and tests for high-complexity merge requests, under your model-selection controls. Clearer decisions on the merge request. GitLab Duo will be able to approve or request changes under settings you control. Focus on risk. Risk assessment on the merge request will help teams see which changes deserve more attention. Review before the merge request opens. Local review in Duo CLI will let developers run project review guidance against working-tree changes before the merge request runs the organization’s official check. As agents write more of your code, you need reviewed code reaching production, with every change held to your standards and your reviewers focused on the changes that need a person. Every improvement on this roadmap is built to help you get there. Getting started If you are new to GitLab Duo Agent Platform, you can get access with a free trial . If you already are a GitLab Premium or Ultimate customer, you can simply turn on Duo Agent Platform and use the GitLab Credits included with your subscription . items.title: Gemini 4 Argon on GitLab: Built for long-running agentic work
items.author: Brittany Lutz https://about.gitlab.com/blog/authors/brittany-lutz/
items.summary: As AI models take on longer, multi-step work, the challenge is putting that power to use across the software lifecycle without adding risk or cost. Teams need to be able to move faster, within enterprise controls and guardrails. Google's Gemini 4 Argon, now available on GitLab Duo Agent Platform , was built for that kind of work. With Argon, your team can delegate long, multi-step actions and receive outputs for review. In GitLab's internal evaluation, Gemini 4 Argon completed 93.3% of GitLab’s software engineering benchmark tasks. Reliable execution for long-horizon tasks Work across the software lifecycle demands persistence and steady attention. Argon sustains its reasoning across the many steps of a task, reading files, running commands, and editing code through to completion. Your engineers can delegate to GitLab Duo agents powered by Argon with confidence and spend their time reviewing results instead of monitoring runs. Google trained Argon to respect system boundaries, tell you when it couldn't find something or finish a task, and pause for confirmation before an irreversible step. Teams can hand off complex tasks and stay in control of the important decisions. In internal evaluations, Argon resolved 73.3% of GitLab’s benchmark tasks , with each change passing the benchmark’s tests across multiple programming languages. Of the runs that hit a tool error or timeout, Argon still completed 93.8% of them, so a single failure mid-run won’t force your team to start over. Agent output lands in a merge request, where your team reviews the result with the full context of the change. Argon works through problems thoroughly, making it a strong model choice when finishing correctly matters more than finishing fast. Choose the Gemini model that fits your workload Gemini 4 Argon is Google's newest frontier model and the most performant Gemini model on GitLab Duo Agent Platform. It handles long-horizon agentic actions especially well, including tasks that begin loosely defined. It pairs with the Flash models, which offer a lower-cost option for high-volume work, so you can match each workload to the best Gemini model. Whichever Gemini model you choose, it runs inside the same context layer, policy checks, and audit trail that cover every agentic action across your software lifecycle. Argon is available at promotional pricing of 2.86 calls per credit , through November 30, 2026. Starting December 1, standard pricing applies at 1.33 calls per credit. If you already use GitLab Duo Agent Platform, you can try Argon today by choosing Gemini 4 Argon in model selection . items.author: Zachary Chen
items.summary: Cat Jam is now available on AI Gateway as a stealth model, free to use during the stealth period. Cat Jam is a reasoning model for coding and agentic tasks, with low-latency inference. It supports function calling , so agents can connect it to your own tools, and structured outputs that follow a JSON schema you supply. Responses include the model's reasoning text alongside the answer. Cat Jam takes text input only. Cat Jam supports low , medium , high , xhigh , and max reasoning efforts. Zero Data Retention (ZDR) is not available for this model. Prompts may be retained for safety reasons. Cat Jam works with the AI SDK , the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, the Anthropic-compatible Messages API , and coding agents connected to AI Gateway. Use stealth /cat-jam as the model name: To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup: Then select stealth/cat-jam in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details. Try Cat Jam in the model playground . AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting , budgets for API keys , routing rules , and more. AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.
